author: Our World in Data
body:
Differences in GDP per capita across sub-Saharan Africa are large.

Sub-Saharan Africa is the world’s poorest region. Its GDP per person is around $5,000 a year — less than a quarter of the global average of around $22,000.

But looking at the region as a whole can make it easy to forget just how different the economies within it are. That’s what this chart shows, by ranking GDP per capita across sub-Saharan African countries.

These differences are large. At the top of the chart, Gabon has a GDP per capita of about $19,000, roughly 18 times that of Burundi at the bottom. The gap between the richest and poorest countries in sub-Saharan Africa is even larger than the gap between the region and the world as a whole.

(written by Esteban Ortiz-Ospina)

Read more about what GDP is and why it matters: https://ourworldindata.org/what-is-economic-growth

author: Our World in Data
body:
What does poverty look like beyond income?

Someone can live above an income poverty line and still go without electricity, clean drinking water, or schooling.

The global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), from the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative and the UN Development Programme, counts the deprivations people face at the same time. We recently updated our 16 charts with the 2026 release, published in October, which adds new surveys for 13 countries.

The MPI looks at ten indicators in three areas, using data from household surveys: health (nutrition and child mortality), education (years of schooling and school attendance), and living standards (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and assets). People deprived in a third or more of the weighted indicators count as “multidimensionally poor”. You can read more about how the MPI works in our article.

The chart shows this for Nigeria, which has a new survey from 2024. About half of Nigerians live in a household without electricity, about half in one without adequate sanitation, and more than three-quarters in one that cooks with solid fuels like wood or charcoal. 12% live in a household where a child has died in the previous five years.

(This data update was led by Pablo Arriagada.)

Explore all of the updated data in our interactive charts: https://ourworldindata.org/search?datasetProducts=Global+Multidimensional+Poverty+Index+%28MPI%29

author: Our World in Data
body:
How much CO2 can the world emit while limiting global temperature rise?

In 2015, countries worldwide signed the Paris Agreement, aiming to keep the global temperature rise “well below 2°C” and to limit it to 1.5°C.

To meet these targets, there are limits to the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) that can be emitted. These are called carbon budgets. Every year we emit more CO2, these budgets shrink.

In the chart, you can see estimates for how much CO2 the world can emit while staying below different levels of warming. This is based on a 50% likelihood of staying below it; if we wanted to guarantee we wouldn’t exceed these temperatures, our budget would be much smaller.

For perspective, we’ve compared each budget with the projected amount of CO2 that the world is expected to emit in 2026. This tells us how many years we have left if emissions stay at their current levels.

At current emission rates, the 1.5°C budget would run out around 2030. It seems implausible that global emissions will fall quickly enough to avoid this.

The 2°C budget would last until mid-century. By taking action on climate change, we buy ourselves more time and can avoid this level of warming.

(written by Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Rosado)

This is based on the latest estimates from the Global Carbon Project. See how emissions are changing in your country: https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/co2

Other sources & data:

https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-paris-agreement

https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/18/3889/2026/

https://globalcarbonbudget.org/

author: Our World in Data
body:
Explore the age and sex profile of immigrants in each country with our new interactive tool.

The age and sex profile of immigrants often differs from that of the native-born population, and this can vary from country to country. We’ve built an interactive population pyramid that allows you to compare the two.

In this example, the blue (men) and red (women) bars show the demographic profile of the immigrant population living in the United States. This is stacked by age, with the youngest at the bottom and the oldest at the top. By default, the tool shows each group’s share of the total immigrant population.

The black line shows the native-born population for comparison.

In most countries, immigrants are more likely than native-born people to be of working age, often because they’ve come to work or study. So compared with the black line, the bars tend to be wider in the middle and narrower at the bottom.

Using our interactive tool, you can look at this data for many countries and see how things have changed over time. You can also find this tool on the new version of our migration page.

(This featured viz was created by Hannah Ritchie and Sophia Mersmann.)

Compare immigrants and native-born people in your country: https://ourworldindata.org/country-by-country-whats-the-age-and-sex-profile-of-immigrant-populations
